knowledge: A workflow orchestrates model calls and tools through predefined code paths; an agent dynamically decides its own steps and tool use based on what it learns.
Agents trade higher cost, latency and unpredictability for flexibility, so they are justified only when the number or order of steps cannot be fixed in advance.

Common workflow patterns: prompt chaining (fixed sequence with gates), routing (classify then hand off), parallelization (independent subtasks or voting), orchestrator-workers, and evaluator-optimizer (generate, critique, refine).
In a manager/supervisor hierarchy, the supervisor decomposes the task, delegates to specialist workers with clear objectives and scopes, and synthesizes their results.
Subagents run in their own fresh context and return only their result, which isolates exploration from the main context and lets independent work run in parallel.
Multi-agent systems usually use more tokens in total and fit broad, separable tasks; tightly interdependent work such as editing one coupled module suits a single agent better.
skills: Decide between a workflow and an agent from how predictable the steps are and how much auditability is required.
Pick the right workflow pattern (chaining, routing, parallelization, evaluator-optimizer) for a described task.
Write delegation instructions that give each subagent an objective, a non-overlapping scope and an output format.
Design subagents to return condensed, structured results rather than raw exploration output.
Route simple requests around an expensive hierarchy so complexity matches each request.
examLens: Start with the simplest design that meets the requirement; add agentic autonomy only when the path genuinely cannot be fixed in code.
Duplicate work or coverage gaps in a hierarchy point to vague delegation, not to too few agents or too small a model.
Use subagents for context isolation and parallelism on separable work, and expect higher total token cost.
traps: Over-engineering: a supervisor with many subagents for a fixed three-step process.
Assuming subagents inherit the parent's conversation or that splitting work always lowers cost.
Fixing coordination problems by adding more agents or a bigger model instead of clearer task boundaries.

knowledge: The Claude Agent SDK (Python and TypeScript) provides the same built-in tools, agent loop, context management, permissions, sessions and hooks that power Claude Code; it runs and supervises a Claude Code process.

The Client SDK calls the Claude API directly: you write the tool loop yourself (or use its tool runner), handling `stop_reason` `tool_use` by returning `tool_result` blocks that reference each `tool_use_id`.

Deployment models: self-host the Agent SDK in sandboxed containers you operate (ephemeral, long-running or hybrid patterns), or use Claude Managed Agents, where a hosted harness runs the loop and sessions run in an Anthropic-managed or self-hosted sandbox.
Hooks are code that runs deterministically at agent events such as `PreToolUse` (can block or modify a call) and `PostToolUse` (after execution, for logging or follow-up).
The SDK checks hooks first, then permission rules; a hook returning `allow` does not bypass deny rules, and `canUseTool` handles runtime approval for anything rules do not settle.
By default `query()` loads the same filesystem settings as the CLI (CLAUDE.md, project settings, `.claude/` skills and agents); `settingSources: []` limits the agent to programmatic configuration.
skills: Choose between the Agent SDK, the Client SDK with a custom loop, and Managed Agents for a given set of build and operations constraints.
Implement a correct tool-use loop that continues while `stop_reason` is `tool_use`.
Use `PreToolUse` hooks to enforce must-never-happen rules and `PostToolUse` hooks for complete audit logs.
Restrict tools to least privilege and add human approval for sensitive tools with `canUseTool`.
Use session resume to continue work and session fork to explore alternatives without altering the original history.
Isolate multi-tenant SDK deployments with per-tenant file systems and explicit `settingSources`.
examLens: When a requirement must hold every time, choose a hook or permission rule over a prompt instruction.
Pick the hosting model by who should operate the infrastructure: Managed Agents to offload it, self-hosted SDK containers for full control.
A loop that stops after Claude says it will use a tool is missing the execute-and-return `tool_result` step.
traps: Using a `PostToolUse` hook to prevent an action; it fires after the tool has already run.
Relying on system-prompt rules, temperature or turn limits as security controls.
Treating the Agent SDK as a stateless HTTP client that needs no shell or file system.

knowledge: In a tool-use loop, Claude requests a tool call, the application executes it and returns a `tool_result`, and the loop repeats until Claude finishes; failures should come back as informative error results.
Context is a finite resource: compaction summarizes older turns, and context editing can clear stale tool results in long runs.
The Messages API is stateless; the memory tool lets Claude read and write memory files that the application stores in infrastructure it controls.
Just-in-time retrieval keeps lightweight references (paths, titles) in context and loads full content with tools only when needed.
Structured note-taking (for example a progress file) keeps long-horizon state outside the context window so it survives compaction.
Frameworks such as LangGraph (graph-based stateful orchestration), PydanticAI (type-validated outputs) and Strands add useful abstractions, but can obscure the prompts and calls underneath.
skills: Build a bounded tool-use loop with error results and a maximum iteration count.
Choose between compaction, tool-result clearing, note-taking and subagents to manage a growing context.
Add cross-session memory to an API-based agent without relying on the model to remember.
Decide whether a framework is warranted or whether direct API calls are simpler.
Debug framework-based agents by inspecting the actual requests sent to Claude.
examLens: Start with direct API calls and adopt a framework only when its specific capabilities are needed.
Keep context small and relevant: retrieve on demand, clear what is stale, and persist durable state outside the window.
Bound every loop deterministically and surface tool failures to the model so it can adapt.
traps: A bigger context window or model as the fix for context bloat.
Believing frameworks are required for tool use or that they guarantee lower token cost.
Assuming the API remembers earlier conversations without an explicit memory mechanism.

knowledge: CLAUDE.md hierarchy: managed policy, user (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`), project (`./CLAUDE.md`, shared via git) and `CLAUDE.local.md` for personal project notes kept out of git; files above the working directory load at launch and subdirectory files load on demand.
`.claude/rules/` files with `paths` frontmatter load only when Claude works with matching files; rules without `paths` load unconditionally, and `@` imports do not reduce context cost.
CLAUDE.md is context, not enforced configuration; use hooks or permission rules for anything that must always hold.
Settings precedence, highest first: managed settings, command-line arguments, `.claude/settings.local.json`, `.claude/settings.json`, `~/.claude/settings.json`.
Skills (`.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`) create slash commands; custom commands have been merged into skills, and `disable-model-invocation: true` makes a skill user-triggered only.
Headless mode is `claude -p`; `--output-format json` returns one result and `stream-json` streams events; auto mode uses a classifier model to review actions instead of prompting.
skills: Place an instruction in the right CLAUDE.md scope or path-scoped rule.
Run `/init` to bootstrap a CLAUDE.md, and use `/compact`, `/clear` and `/resume` to manage sessions.
Choose the settings file scope for personal, team and organization-enforced configuration.

Package a repeatable procedure as a skill and control who can invoke it.
Pick a permission mode (manual, accept edits, plan, auto, bypass) for a situation.
examLens: Shared team conventions go in committed files; personal ones go in local, git-ignored files.
Guarantees come from hooks, permission rules or managed settings, never from wording in CLAUDE.md.
Load context only when relevant: path-scoped rules and skills over an ever-growing root CLAUDE.md.
traps: Putting personal or secret values in the committed project CLAUDE.md or settings.json.
Choosing bypass permissions when the requirement is fewer prompts with risky actions still reviewed.
